            I.       INTRODUCTION

       Ten parties (the “Signatories”) 1 reached the June 22, 2026, Comprehensive Stipulation

(“Stipulation”) after discovery, testimony, and arm’s-length bargaining. Commission Utility

Division Staff (“Staff”) nevertheless asks the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission

(“Commission”) to rewrite that bargain around Staff’s litigation positions. Staff stands alone in

asking the Commission to reject or materially revise the negotiated result.

       The Commission should not derail the Signatories’ significant efforts to reach a

Comprehensive Stipulation that, without question, is in the public interest. The Stipulation cuts

SPS’s requested base-rate increase by nearly half, adds meaningful customer protections, supports

reliable service for growing New Mexico load, and resolves the case through an integrated

compromise supported by the record. Simply put, the evidence demonstrates that the Stipulation

meets all of the Commission’s settlement criteria. The Stipulation:

       •        resulted from serious bargaining among capable, knowledgeable parties;

       •        benefits customers and the public interest when viewed as a whole;

       •        violates no important regulatory principle or practice; and

       •        results in rates that are “fair, just, and reasonable.”

The Commission should approve the Stipulation in its entirety and without modification.

       The record shows that the Stipulation delivers substantial benefits to customers. It allows

SPS to continue to provide safe and reliable service while reducing SPS’s original requested base-

rate increase by nearly half, from $175.4 million to $90 million. It also reduces SPS’s requested

return on equity and equity ratio, sets cash working capital at zero, and withdraws SPS’s requests

          II.    THE RECORD ANSWERS CHAIR O’CONNELL’S QUESTIONS ABOUT
                THE FAIRNESS OF THE STIPULATED RATES

        Before turning to Staff’s specific objections, the Commission should first address the two

threshold fairness questions raised at hearing. Those questions frame the analysis that follows: the

Commission reviews the stipulated rates by their total effect under New Mexico law, not by

isolating individual terms or comparing New Mexico retail rates to Texas retail rates. A shared

electric system does not require identical retail rates.

                A. “Fair, Just, and Reasonable” establishes a single approval standard.

        New Mexico law imposes one rate-approval standard. Section 62-3-1(B) of the Public

Utility Act (“PUA”) declares New Mexico’s policy to ensure adequate utility service at “fair, just,

and reasonable rates.” That provision requires the Commission to balance customers’, investors’,

and the public’s interests, while encouraging needed investment. Section 62-8-1 similarly requires

every utility rate to be “just and reasonable.” 15 These provisions establish one flexible, end-result

standard: whether the resulting rates reasonably balance the interests the PUA protects. Nothing in

either provision requires a distinct meaning or separate evidentiary showing for each term.

        The ordinary meaning of “fair” supports that conclusion. 16 Black’s Law Dictionary defines

“fair” as “impartial; just; equitable; disinterested.” In other words, “fair” substantially overlaps

with “just.” It does not impose a separate ratemaking requirement beyond what is “just and

reasonable.”

        New Mexico Supreme Court precedent establishes the contours of a “just and reasonable”

rate. A just and reasonable rate balances customer and investor interests 17 and must fall within a

           The Hearing Examiners also asked whether the Energy-at-Source allocator fairly allocates

PTCs when different customer classes pay different average prices per kWh. The answer follows

from the nature of the credit. The Internal Revenue Code calculates the amount of a PTC by

multiplying eligible kilowatt-hours of electricity by the applicable credit rate. The amount of the

credit therefore turns on energy production, not retail revenue, or the price a customer pays.125

Consistent with that relationship, Section 1.8 allocates the new solar PTCs on the same Energy-at-

Source basis SPS has long used for PTCs from the Hale and Sagamore Wind Projects.

           The Energy-at-Source allocator tracks the relationship between energy consumption and

the resulting benefit. SPS begins with each class’s metered kWh, adjusts that usage for the line

losses SPS incurs to serve each voltage class, and allocates the PTCs according to each class’s

share of the resulting source energy. The loss adjustment converts each class’s metered usage to

its generation-level equivalent, placing all voltage classes on the same generation-level basis. Each

class thus receives a share of the PTC value associated with the amount of electricity SPS must

generate to serve it. Because SPS incurs greater losses when serving lower-voltage customers,

those customers receive more PTC value per metered kWh than customers served at higher

voltages. 126

           By contrast, a class’s average retail price per kWh does not determine the PTCs attributable

to serving that class. Retail rates recover customer-related, demand-related, transmission,

distribution, and other costs that do not enter the PTC calculation. Fixed charges, load

characteristics, and rate design also affect a class’s average price. A class may therefore pay a
